title: Can ten lots and three lots of the same number join?
description: Ten times ninety eight and three times ninety eight are written as one product by adding the ten and the three. Fourteen tens take away six tens becomes eight tens in the same way. Keeko doubts that the shared ninety eight must be written twice.
teaching_notes: One idea: the multiple of a sum or a difference is the sum or difference of the multiples, so a shared number is written once outside the bracket. Watch for students who write the shared number inside the bracket twice.

video_script.why: A learner sees why equal lots of one number can be joined into one product, for a sum and for a difference.
video_script.substitution: Replace ninety eight and ten with any shared number and the same bracket works.
video_script.anchor: ninety eight written ten times and three times in a row, and ten written fourteen times with six taken away
video_script.wrong_answer: the common ninety eight must be written twice
video_script.wrong_move: writes the shared 98 inside the bracket as well as outside it, as if both products still needed their own 98
video_script.payoff_line: The two values are one thousand two hundred and seventy four, and eighty.

final_answer.spoken: one thousand two hundred and seventy four, and eighty

maths_rules: 14 times 10 take away 6 times 10 is (14 − 6) = 8 times 10
video_script.design: A row of ninety eights drawn ten and three at a time, then a row of tens drawn fourteen with six taken away. The shared number moves outside one bracket.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a row of ten cards each marked 98 and a second row of three cards each marked 98

marks.h2: the row of ten cards marked 98 appears
marks.h3: the row of three cards marked 98 appears
marks.h4: a question mark glows over both rows

narration: <bookmark mark='h1'/>This is a question from your book about adding equal lots.
<bookmark mark='h2'/>Ten times ninety eight means ninety eight written ten times and added.
<bookmark mark='h3'/>Three times ninety eight means ninety eight written three times and added.
<bookmark mark='h4'/>If we join both rows, how many times is ninety eight written in all?

beats.on_screen: both rows stay on the board and the question mark keeps glowing

marks.t1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='t1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the two rows of 98 joined into one row; the words distributive property written under it

marks.g1: the two rows of 98 slide together into one row
marks.g2: the same joining is shown on a row of tens with some taken away
marks.g3: the words distributive property are written under the rows

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>Equal lots of one number can be joined into one bigger lot.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Equal lots can also be taken away from other equal lots.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>This rule is called the distributive property.
<bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, ten times ninety eight plus three times ninety eight.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>Also given, fourteen times ten minus six times ten.

beats.on_screen: To find: each as one product, and both values

marks.fd1: the words one product are written

narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We have to write each one as a single product and find both values.

marks.s11: the two lots of 98 are boxed together
marks.s12: the 10 and the 3 move into a bracket, with 98 written once outside

narration: <bookmark mark='s11'/>Step one, join the lots of ninety eight, because ten lots and three lots make thirteen lots.
<bookmark mark='s12'/>We have ten times ninety eight plus three times ninety eight.
It equals open bracket ten plus three close bracket times ninety eight.
<bookmark mark='s13'/>This is thirteen times ninety eight.

marks.s21: fourteen tens are drawn with six of them taken away
marks.s22: the 14 and the 6 move into a bracket, with 10 written once outside

narration: <bookmark mark='s21'/>Step two, take away the lots of ten, because fourteen tens take away six tens leave eight tens.
<bookmark mark='s22'/>Fourteen times ten minus six times ten equals open bracket fourteen minus six close bracket times ten.
<bookmark mark='s23'/>This is eight times ten.

beats.on_screen: multiple of a sum = sum of the multiples; multiple of a difference = difference of the multiples

marks.s31: the rule for a sum is written
marks.s32: the rule for a difference is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s31'/>Step three, read the rule in words.
The multiple of a sum is the sum of the multiples.
<bookmark mark='s32'/>The multiple of a difference is the difference of the multiples.
<bookmark mark='s41'/>Step four, find thirteen times ninety eight by opening the bracket again.
<bookmark mark='s42'/>Ten times ninety eight is nine hundred and eighty.
Three times ninety eight is two hundred and ninety four.
<bookmark mark='a1'/>The two values are one thousand two hundred and seventy four, and eighty.
<bookmark mark='a2'/>Thirteen times ninety eight is the first, and eight times ten is the second.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='k1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 98 written twice; it is struck out and a single 98 stands outside the bracket

marks.k3: the second 98 slides out and joins the first
marks.k4: a single 98 stands outside the bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='k2'/>Keeko thinks the common ninety eight must be written twice.
<bookmark mark='k3'/>But ninety eight is the same number in both products.
<bookmark mark='k4'/>A shared number is written once, outside the bracket.
